tldr: By running an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) within a low-dimensional parameter subspace of large neural network reward models, this work achieves both highly accurate uncertainty quantification and extremely fast active learning.
overview:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is a powerful approach for aligning the behaviors of robots and agents. However, preference feedback (pairwise comparisons)—where humans are asked which of two trajectories is better—provides very little information per query, leading to poor sample efficiency and requiring an enormous number of queries. To alleviate this burden, active learning is essential to intelligently select the queries about which the model is most uncertain. However, picking the right queries requires accurately quantifying the prediction uncertainty of neural networks, and the computational cost explodes as models grow larger.

To tackle this, the authors leveraged the property that neural network parameter spaces are redundant and key solutions lie within a much lower-dimensional subspace. The proposed method, PreferenceEKF, avoids operating directly on the full parameter space. Instead, it runs a classic Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) inside a low-dimensional subspace compressed via methods such as principal component analysis. As a result, each time a new preference query arrives, the posterior distribution can be updated instantly via closed-form matrix operations, without retraining on all past data.

Experiments were conducted on the continuous control benchmarks D4RL and V-D4RL (visual inputs). Compared to existing Bayesian deep learning baselines such as Deep Ensembles, Dropout, and MCMC, PreferenceEKF achieved substantially faster runtimes (about 5x faster than Deep Ensembles and 40x faster than LLMCMC) while maintaining superior sample efficiency. Furthermore, when the learned reward models were used in offline reinforcement learning, they yielded policies competitive with those trained on ground-truth environment rewards.
contributions: Proposed PreferenceEKF, the first framework for active reward learning from preferences that runs an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) over a neural network parameter subspace.

Enabled sequential, instantaneous updates of the posterior in a low-dimensional space as each new query arrives—without retraining on all historical data—allowing fast sampling from the posterior without massive computational overhead.

Demonstrated on 12 tasks in the D4RL benchmark that it achieves comparable or superior sample efficiency, excellent calibration, roughly 5x speedups, and favorable scalability compared to Bayesian deep learning baselines.
Showed that the learned reward models achieve policy performance in offline reinforcement learning (IQL) comparable to policies trained with ground-truth rewards or existing methods.

sections.heading: Why use a Kalman filter for active reward learning now?
sections.summary: Active learning is critical to reducing the burden of human feedback in RLHF, but quantifying uncertainty in deep neural networks is computationally heavy. This work achieves efficient posterior inference by projecting parameters into a low-dimensional subspace and applying an Extended Kalman Filter.
sections.details:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become the standard technique for aligning agents with human intent. In particular, preference feedback—where a person compares two trajectories and picks the preferred one—is easy for humans to provide, but each comparison yields at most one bit of information. As a result, thousands of queries are typically needed, making the process impractical.

Active learning is the key to minimizing the required number of queries. The model evaluates its own uncertainty and actively selects and queries the user with the most uncertain trajectories—the ones that yield the most information. However, properly capturing Bayesian uncertainty in deep neural networks (NNs) is notoriously difficult. In practice, ensembles and Dropout are frequently used, but ensembles incur high computational costs because they require training multiple large NNs, while Dropout has been criticized for poor uncertainty approximation.

To solve this dilemma, this work proposes PreferenceEKF. It exploits the insight that while the parameter space of an NN is vast, effective solutions often reside in a much lower-dimensional subspace. By projecting down to a low-dimensional subspace, the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)—a staple in robotics—can be applied to track the posterior sequentially in a lightweight and analytical manner. This makes sampling model parameters for evaluating acquisition functions remarkably simple and fast.

sections.heading: Limitations of prior work and the subspace inference approach
sections.summary: Prior active reward learning relied heavily on linear models or ensembles, facing limits in computational cost and approximation accuracy. This work bridges recent advances in Bayesian deep learning and subspace inference to preference learning.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main areas:

- Reinforcement learning from human preferences and active learning: While learning from expert demonstrations via inverse reinforcement learning was once standard, pairwise trajectory comparisons have recently taken center stage. Bayesian active learning has succeeded with linear models and Gaussian Processes (GPs), but sampling from posteriors of high-dimensional deep NNs is difficult, effectively forcing practitioners to rely on ensembles or Dropout.

- Uncertainty quantification (UQ) in neural networks: Bayesian approaches such as Laplace approximations, variational inference, and MCMC exist, but scaling them to deep models remains challenging. Using Bayesian filters originally designed for state estimation to train NNs has a long history, and combining them with subspace methods has recently reopened the door to deep learning. This work extends that idea to active reward learning.

- Subspace methods: It is well known that the effective number of parameters required to solve a task is far smaller than the total network size. Prior work has explored applying Bayesian inference only to the last layer, or constructing low-dimensional subspaces via singular value decomposition (SVD) of SGD trajectories or random projections. This paper's novelty lies in executing EKF inference over preference data directly within such subspaces.

sections.heading: Fundamentals of preference models and information gain (InfoGain)
sections.summary: Reward learning from preferences uses the Bradley-Terry model, and active learning uses the InfoGain acquisition function, which maximizes mutual information between the query response and model parameters. Computing it requires extensive sampling from the posterior.
sections.details:
### Preference-Based Reward Modeling
The agent's environment is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Given an evaluator with an unknown reward function $r(s)$, two trajectory pairs $Q_i = (\tau_a^i, \tau_b^i)$ are presented, and a binary label $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ indicating which trajectory the evaluator preferred is collected.

This preference probability is formulated via the Bradley-Terry (BT) model:
$$p_\theta(y \mid \tau_a, \tau_b) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-\beta (\mathcal{R}_\theta(\tau_a) - \mathcal{R}_\theta(\tau_b)))}$$
Here, $\mathcal{R}_\theta(\tau)$ is the sum of neural network rewards $r_\theta(s)$ across states in the trajectory, and $\beta$ represents the noise level (temperature parameter) of the evaluator's choices.

### Information-Theoretic Active Learning (InfoGain)
In active learning, an acquisition function is evaluated to decide which trajectory pair $Q_i$ will most effectively identify the reward function. This paper adopts InfoGain, which maximizes the mutual information $I(y_i; \bm{\theta} \mid Q_i, \bm{b}^{i-1})$ between the query answer $y_i$ and the model parameters $\bm{\theta}$.

Computing this mutual information relies on a Monte Carlo approximation using a set of $M$ model parameters $\bm{\Theta}$ sampled from the posterior distribution $\bm{b}^{i-1}$. Unlike with linear models, repeatedly sampling from the posterior of high-dimensional NNs has been computationally prohibitive. PreferenceEKF aims to make this sampling feasible in real time.

sections.heading: How PreferenceEKF works: Running a Kalman filter in a subspace
sections.summary: Instead of using the full high-dimensional parameter space, EKF runs sequentially over a low-dimensional subspace obtained via SVD or random projections. Every time a new query arrives, analytical updates are performed, and models are sampled efficiently to compute the acquisition function.
sections.details:
The core of PreferenceEKF lies in framing sequential Bayesian inference by treating the NN parameters as hidden states and preference labels from the BT model as observations.

### Training Neural Networks with EKF
By setting the model parameter dynamics to an identity map $g(\bm{\theta}) = \bm{\theta}$, using the BT model as the observation function $h(\bm{\theta}, Q)$, and assuming Gaussian noise, the posterior $\bm{b}^i = \mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_i, \bm{\Sigma}_i)$ can be sequentially updated in closed form using an EKF. However, the size of the covariance matrix $\bm{\Sigma}_i$ grows as $O(|\bm{\theta}|^2)$ with the total number of parameters $|\bm{\theta}|$, making computation and memory prohibitive for deep learning.

### Subspace Inference
To address this, the parameter space is restricted to a much lower-dimensional subspace $\bm{z}$ ($|\bm{z}| \ll |\bm{\theta}|$). The affine transformation back to the full parameter space is defined as $\bm{\theta}(\bm{z}) = \mathbf{A}\bm{z} + \bm{\theta}_*$. Here, $\bm{\theta}_*$ is a reference parameter vector obtained from a few SGD steps on warmup data, and $\mathbf{A}$ is a fixed projection matrix derived from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the SGD trajectory (or a random projection matrix).

EKF updates occur entirely inside this low-dimensional subspace. Because the posterior $\bm{b}^i = \mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}_i', \bm{\Sigma}_i')$ only requires a small $|\bm{z}| \times |\bm{z}|$ covariance matrix, computational overhead is drastically reduced.

### Overall Active Learning Workflow
The full loop proceeds as follows:
- 1. Sample $M$ latent parameters $\bm{z}$ from the subspace posterior and project them into the full space $\bm{\theta}$ to reconstruct $M$ reward models.
- 2. Select the query $Q_i$ from a candidate pool that maximizes InfoGain across the $M$ models.
- 3. Receive the label $y_i$ from the human (or oracle).
- 4. Deterministically update the EKF posterior in the subspace using only the latest data pair $(Q_i, y_i)$.

Unlike Deep Ensembles, which rerun gradient descent over all cumulative data at every step, PreferenceEKF updates instantly using only the previous state and the single latest data point.

sections.heading: Benchmark evaluations: Sample efficiency, runtime, and calibration
sections.summary: Evaluated across 12 tasks in D4RL against four Bayesian deep learning baselines. PreferenceEKF delivered comparable or superior sample efficiency, roughly 5x faster training, and superior scalability as model sizes grew, while proving effective in offline RL.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
Evaluations covered 12 tasks across MuJoCo (locomotion), Adroit (hand manipulation), and Maze2D (navigation) from the continuous control benchmark D4RL. The query budget was set to $B=60$, the reward model was a 2-layer MLP with 64 units, and the subspace dimension was $|\bm{z}|=200$. Comparisons were made against four methods: DeepEnsemble (5 models), Dropout, Laplace approximation, and LLMCMC (last-layer MCMC).

### 5.1 Sample Efficiency Evaluation
Evaluating test log-likelihood aggregated across all tasks revealed that active learning with PreferenceEKF achieved sample efficiency comparable to or higher than all baselines. Furthermore, the InfoGain acquisition function consistently outperformed Disagreement and Entropy.

### 5.2 Runtime and Scalability
PreferenceEKF demonstrated overwhelmingly faster runtimes. It was approximately 5x faster than DeepEnsemble and more than 40x faster than LLMCMC, which requires many steps for MCMC convergence. In scaling experiments increasing sample size $M$ and network parameter counts, PreferenceEKF's runtime grew most gracefully, showing its robustness to model scaling.

### 5.3 Calibration
To assess uncertainty quality, Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier scores were measured. PreferenceEKF achieved the lowest ECE among all methods (meaning predicted probabilities matched actual accuracy best) and placed second in Brier score, showing high-quality uncertainty estimation.

### 5.4 Subspace Construction Ablation
Investigating subspace dimensionality and construction techniques revealed that SVD is superior at smaller dimensions, but random projections match or surpass SVD as the dimension grows. This demonstrates that random projections can be used even when no initial dataset is available for warmup SGD.

### 5.5 & 5.6 Application to Offline RL, Images, and Sparse Feedback
When offline reinforcement learning (IQL) was trained using the learned reward models, the resulting policies achieved returns comparable to those trained with ground-truth (GT) rewards. The method also proved effective on sparse task success/failure feedback from real-robot data (SOAR) and on image-input tasks when combined with pre-trained visual embeddings.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: Scaling to foundation models
sections.summary: Subspace EKF dramatically speeds up and improves the accuracy of active reward modeling in deep networks. Future work includes handling diverse, multimodal human preferences and scaling to massive foundation models.
sections.details:
This study demonstrates that running an Extended Kalman Filter over a low-dimensional subspace of a neural network dramatically boosts the efficiency of preference-based active reward learning. The ability to update the posterior sequentially from a single new query—without repeatedly retraining multiple models like ensembles—is practically valuable for interactive robot learning and reducing human annotator burden.

### Limitations and Future Work
Several challenges remain:
- Handling diverse evaluators (multimodality): Because EKF assumes a unimodal Gaussian posterior, it struggles to capture multimodal preference distributions where opinions sharply diverge among annotators. Combining this with non-parametric methods like particle filters is a promising direction.
- Applying to ultra-large models: Experiments in this paper were limited to models with hundreds of thousands of parameters. Whether subspace methods scale effectively to foundation-model-scale reward models with billions of parameters remains unverified.
- Interacting with RL policies: Future work could build an integrated framework where the posterior uncertainty of the reward model directly guides RL policy exploration or protects against reward hacking.

takeaways: Leveraging the fact that NN solutions reside in low-dimensional subspaces enables classical Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) to perform fast, analytical sequential Bayesian inference even on deep models.
Because the posterior updates analytically from just a single new data point, active learning runs about 5x faster than deep ensembles that rerun SGD over all past data.
Subspace bases can be built via random projections as well as SVD, allowing flexible application even in settings without warmup training datasets.
The learned reward models exhibit well-calibrated prediction probabilities and yield high-quality policies in offline RL comparable to those trained on ground-truth rewards.
limitations: Because EKF assumes a Gaussian (unimodal) distribution, it is ill-suited for representing multimodal preference data where different human evaluators have conflicting preferences.

Directly handling high-dimensional inputs such as images causes computational explosions during the EKF observation update, making dimension reduction via pre-trained feature extractors a prerequisite.
It has not yet been verified whether compressing the parameter space to hundreds of dimensions remains effective for foundation models with tens of billions of parameters.
